specPoints.text: demonstrate an understanding of Newton’s third law

primer.text: The Momentum lessons have already shown you what momentum is, how collisions conserve it, and how F = ma ties force to changing motion. One question remains: when two bodies interact, how do the forces they feel compare? Newton's third law answers with one symmetric statement about interacting objects, and this note also trains you to tell true third law pairs apart from merely balanced forces.

lessons.title: What is Newton's third law?
sourceHeadings: Newton's third law of motion applied to walking
lessons.opening: Every push or pull is one half of a deal: when object A acts on object B, object B acts back on A. Newton's third law states that the two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction. This lesson builds the statement, tests it on walking, and separates it from the laws describing single objects.
keyPoints: Newton's third law describes the forces that appear when two different objects interact with each other.
Newton's first and second laws instead cover forces acting on just one object.
When any two objects interact, each exerts on the other a force equal in size and opposite in direction.
Walking works because your foot pushes backwards on the ground while the ground pushes forwards on your foot.
The two interacting objects here are the foot and the ground, pushing on each other with equal strength.

low.restatement: Push on something and it pushes back on you just as hard, the other way.
low.analogy: It is like leaning on a wall: your lean is matched, newton for newton, by the wall pushing back on you.
low.examPointer: Name both objects when describing a third law pair — 'A pushes B, B pushes A' earns the marking points.

medium.restatement: The law pairs forces, not objects: each body feels one force of the pair, equal in size, opposite in direction.
medium.analogy: Picture a mirrored handshake: whatever force one hand delivers, the other hand delivers straight back, flipped.
medium.examPointer: The pair acts on two different objects — claiming both forces act on one object is the classic marking trap.

check.stem: Newton's third law of motion describes:

options.text: The motion of a single object under one named force
options.explanation: That is the territory of Newton's first and second laws.

options.text: How energy transfers between two objects
options.explanation: Energy is not what the law describes — forces are.

options.text: The forces that arise when two different objects interact
options.explanation: Interactions between two different objects are exactly its subject matter.

options.text: Why objects keep moving when no force acts
options.explanation: Persistent motion with no force is Newton's first law instead.

check.stem: Two objects interact. Compared with the force the first exerts on the second, the force the second exerts on the first is:

options.text: Equal in size and opposite in direction
options.explanation: That symmetry is precisely what the law guarantees.

options.text: Equal in size and in the same direction
options.explanation: The pair points opposite ways, never the same way.

options.text: Smaller, because it acts later
options.explanation: The pair appears together; neither force waits its turn.

options.text: Larger if the first object is heavier
options.explanation: The objects' masses never rescale the mutual forces.

check.stem: During walking, the force that pushes you forwards is:

options.text: The push of your foot on the ground
options.explanation: That push lands on the ground, not on you.

options.text: A forward drag from the air
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario has the air driving you forwards.

options.text: The push of the ground on your foot
options.explanation: The ground's forward push on your foot is the partner of your backward push.

options.text: Gravity pulling you along the road
options.explanation: Weight points downwards; it has no forwards part on level ground.

check.stem: Newton's first law differs from his third because the first concerns:

options.text: Forces exchanged between two objects
options.explanation: Exchanged forces are the third law's territory.

options.text: Forces acting on just one object
options.explanation: The first law tracks the balance of forces on a single body.

options.text: Only objects already moving uniformly
options.explanation: The first law covers resting objects too.

options.text: Forces that never balance
options.explanation: Forces on one body can certainly balance.

check.stem: A foot pushes backwards on the ground. The ground's push on the foot acts on:

options.text: A different object: the foot
options.explanation: Third law pushes always land on the two different objects involved.

options.text: The ground itself, so the pushes could cancel
options.explanation: The ground feels the foot's push; the foot feels the ground's push.

options.text: Only the whole Earth
options.explanation: The push acts on the foot itself, wherever it stands.

options.text: Nothing, because the pushes cancel
options.explanation: Forces on different objects cannot cancel one another.

check.stem: State Newton's third law of motion.
check.modelAnswer: When any two objects interact, each exerts on the other a force that is equal in size and opposite in direction.

check.stem: Which two objects interact to make walking possible, and what does each one do?
check.modelAnswer: The foot and the ground: your foot pushes backwards on the ground, and the ground pushes forwards on your foot with an equal force.

check.stem: Explain why pushing backwards on the ground moves you forwards.
check.modelAnswer: Your foot pushes backwards on the ground, so by Newton's third law the ground pushes forwards on your foot with an equal, opposite force; that forward push is what drives you along.

check.stem: A swimmer pushes the water backwards. Describe the partner force and its effect on the swimmer.
check.modelAnswer: The water pushes the swimmer forwards with an equal, opposite force, and that forward push drives the swimmer through the pool.

lessons.title: Recognising Newton's third law
lessons.opening: Equal and opposite forces appear in two very different situations: balanced forces on one object, and third law pairs across two objects. Confusing them is one of the most common exam errors. This lesson gives you a three-part test, then works a full example with a book resting on a table.
keyPoints: A third law pair acts on two different objects, one force on each body.
The pair's two forces are always equal in size and opposite in direction.
Both forces in the pair must be the same type, such as two weights or two contact pushes.
If naming a force proves difficult, describe it simply as a push or a pull.
A book resting on a table feels its weight and the table's contact push, and both act on the book alone.
Those two book forces are balanced, so they illustrate Newton's first law rather than the third.

low.restatement: Run the three checks: different objects, equal-and-opposite, and the same force type.
low.analogy: Matching a third law pair is like pairing socks: same kind, equal size, opposite feet.
low.examPointer: Always ask which two objects feel the forces — one body only means balanced forces, not a pair.

medium.restatement: Balanced forces mimic a third law pair because both are equal and opposite; the object count and the force type separate them.
medium.analogy: Two bookends bracing one book versus two people leaning back-to-back: one body shares the forces, the other splits them.
medium.examPointer: The book-on-table diagram is Newton's first law in disguise — expect an exam question asking exactly that.

check.stem: For two forces to qualify as a third law pair, they must act on:

options.text: Two different objects
options.explanation: One force of the pair lands on each of the two bodies.

options.text: The same object
options.explanation: Forces sharing one object describe balance instead.

options.text: Objects with equal masses
options.explanation: The objects' masses play no role in pair membership.

options.text: Objects touching each other
options.explanation: Gravitational pairs act at a distance with no contact.

check.stem: Besides being equal and opposite, the two forces of a third law pair must also be:

options.text: Of different types
options.explanation: The rule demands matching types — two weights, two pushes.

options.text: Both gravitational
options.explanation: Contact-type pairs are just as legitimate.

options.text: Perpendicular to each other
options.explanation: Opposite directions cannot be perpendicular.

options.text: Of the same type
options.explanation: Same-type membership is the third recognition rule.

check.stem: A book rests on a table. Its weight and the table's upward push on it:

options.text: Form a third law pair because they are equal and opposite
options.explanation: Equal and opposite alone is not enough — both forces land on the book.

options.text: Are equal and opposite but act on one object, so they are not a third law pair
options.explanation: Same object plus different types means balanced forces, not a pair.

options.text: Add to a downward resultant
options.explanation: The book is in equilibrium, so the resultant is zero.

options.text: Act on the table and the Earth respectively
options.explanation: Both labelled forces act on the book itself.

check.stem: Which force is the true third law partner of the book's weight?

options.text: The table's push on the book
options.explanation: That push lands on the book and is a contact type — wrong on both counts.

options.text: The book's push on the table
options.explanation: That is the partner of the table's push, not of the weight.

options.text: The book's own gravitational pull on the Earth
options.explanation: Both are weight-type forces, equal and opposite, on two different objects.

options.text: The upward push of the surrounding air
options.explanation: Air plays no part in this gravitational pair.

check.stem: Equal, opposite forces that both act on one object demonstrate:

options.text: Newton's third law
options.explanation: The third law requires two different objects.

options.text: Newton's first law: the object is in equilibrium
options.explanation: Zero resultant force means steady motion or rest.

options.text: Newton's second law producing acceleration
options.explanation: Zero resultant gives zero acceleration, not a second law case.

options.text: A third law pair living on one object
options.explanation: A pair cannot occupy a single object by definition.

check.stem: List the three checks that identify a third law pair.
check.modelAnswer: They act on different objects, they are equal in size and opposite in direction, and they are the same type of force.

check.stem: In the book-on-table example, Student A claims the diagram shows Newton's third law. Who is correct, and why?
check.modelAnswer: Student B is correct: the two forces act on the same object and are of different types, so the diagram shows balanced forces — Newton's first law — rather than a third law pair.

check.stem: Explain why the weight and the table's push on a resting book are not a third law pair.
check.modelAnswer: Both forces act on the same object — the book — and they are different types of force (weight vs contact push). A third law pair requires two different objects and a single force type.

check.stem: A pupil argues: 'The Earth pulls you downwards, so the ground pushing you upwards is Newton's third law.' Give the true partner of your weight to correct them.
check.modelAnswer: The ground's upward push acts on you and is a contact force, so it cannot partner your weight. Your weight's genuine partner is the gravitational pull you exert on the Earth — the same type of force, equal and opposite, acting on a different object.

lessons.title: Newton's third law in collisions
sourceHeadings: Newton's third law applied to a collision
lessons.opening: Collisions make Newton's third law vivid: during the crash, each trolley pushes the other with an equal, opposite force. Yet the two vehicles do not, in general, accelerate equally, because F = ma brings mass into the outcome. This lesson follows a collision from force pair to momentum change to acceleration.
keyPoints: When two objects collide, each exerts on the other an equal force in the opposite direction.
In a collision one object generally gains momentum and speeds up while the other loses momentum and slows down.
For trolleys A and B the pair is written F(B–A) = −F(A–B): same size, opposite signs.
Equal forces do not ensure equal accelerations, because F = ma makes acceleration depend on mass as well.
Equal masses give equal accelerations; unequal masses give unequal accelerations.

low.restatement: During any collision, each body pushes the other equally hard in the opposite direction.
low.analogy: Two skaters shoving off each other feel the same shove, yet the lighter one flies away faster.
low.examPointer: Equal forces never mean equal accelerations — the lighter body accelerates more.

medium.restatement: The third law guarantees the force pair in every collision; F = ma then sets each body's own acceleration from its own mass.
medium.analogy: Same punch, two boxers: the force pair is symmetric, but how each mass responds to its copy of the force is not.
medium.examPointer: Pair 'equal and opposite forces' with 'unequal accelerations' and justify with F = ma — a favourite exam combination.

check.stem: Trolleys A and B collide. The force of A on B, compared with the force of B on A, is:

options.text: Larger in size on the faster trolley
options.explanation: Impact speed does not rescale the mutual pair.

options.text: Smaller in size on the heavier trolley
options.explanation: Each trolley feels the same push size while they interact.

options.text: Zero, because the two pushes cancel
options.explanation: They act on different trolleys, so they cannot cancel.

options.text: Equal in size and opposite in direction
options.explanation: The interaction is a third law pair: equal and opposite.

check.stem: When two trolleys collide, one gains momentum and speeds up; the other usually:

options.text: Slows down, losing momentum
options.explanation: Momentum generally passes across the interaction: one gains, the other loses.

options.text: Speeds up as well
options.explanation: The interaction generally slows the second trolley rather than speeding it up.

options.text: Keeps exactly the same momentum
options.explanation: The contact forces change both trolleys' momenta.

options.text: Stops dead, losing all its momentum
options.explanation: A collision changes momentum; it need not erase it.

check.stem: The relationship between the two collision forces is written:

options.text: F(B–A) = F(A–B)
options.explanation: The minus sign matters — the pushes point opposite ways.

options.text: F(B–A) = −F(A–B), but only when the masses are equal
options.explanation: The pair holds whatever masses the trolleys have.
The mutual forces exist exactly while the trolleys interact.

options.text: F(B–A) = −F(A–B)
options.explanation: Equal magnitude, opposite sign — the third law in symbols.

check.stem: Two trolleys of equal mass collide. During the impact their accelerations are:

options.text: Zero, because the forces cancel
options.explanation: The forces act on different trolleys and cannot cancel on either one.

options.text: Equal, because equal masses feel equal forces
options.explanation: With F = ma, equal force and equal mass give equal acceleration.

options.text: Different, because the trolleys move differently
options.explanation: A velocity difference is not an acceleration difference.

options.text: Whatever caused the collision decides
options.explanation: The force pair is symmetric; history does not enter F = ma.

check.stem: A heavy trolley and a light trolley collide. During the impact:

options.text: The light trolley feels the larger force
options.explanation: The mutual forces are equal whatever the masses.

options.text: Both feel equal forces and accelerate equally
options.explanation: Equal forces on unequal masses cannot give equal accelerations.

options.text: The forces are equal, but the light trolley accelerates more
options.explanation: Same force and smaller mass give the larger acceleration, from F = ma.

options.text: The heavy trolley feels no force at all
options.explanation: Both bodies feel the pair for as long as they touch.

check.stem: State what Newton's third law says about the forces when two trolleys collide.
check.modelAnswer: Each trolley exerts on the other a force equal in size and opposite in direction, so F(B–A) = −F(A–B).

check.stem: What decides each trolley's acceleration in a collision, and when are two accelerations equal?
check.modelAnswer: F = ma sets it: acceleration depends on the force and on the trolley's mass, so equal masses give equal accelerations while unequal masses give unequal accelerations.

check.stem: Explain why colliding trolleys feel equal forces yet can accelerate unequally.
check.modelAnswer: The third law fixes the force pair as equal and opposite, but each acceleration comes from F = ma with that trolley's own mass, so the lighter trolley accelerates more.

check.stem: Trolley A (2 kg) collides with trolley B (1 kg). At one instant the force of A on B is 6 N. State the force of B on A, and calculate each trolley's acceleration at that instant.
check.modelAnswer: By Newton's third law the force of B on A is 6 N in the opposite direction. Then a(A) = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 m/s² and a(B) = 6 ÷ 1 = 6 m/s² — the lighter trolley accelerates more.

glossary.definition: Interacting objects exert on each other forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
A diagram showing every force acting on one chosen object.
Two forces of the same type, equal in size and opposite in direction, acting on two different objects.
Forces on a single object whose overall effect is zero, such as a book resting on a table.
The perpendicular push that a surface exerts on an object resting on it.
The quantity of motion carried by a moving object; in collisions one body gains it as the other loses it.

workedExample.prompt: A physics textbook rests on a table. Student A sketches the free-body diagram of the book, labelling the weight and the reaction force, and says it shows Newton's third law in action. Student B disagrees. Referring to the vector diagram, work out which student is right and why.
steps: Identify the forces: the Earth pulls the book downwards (its weight) and the table pushes the book upwards (the normal contact force).
State the law: whenever two bodies interact, the mutual forces are equal in size and opposite in direction.
Test the diagram against the recognition rules: both arrows act on the book alone, and the forces are of different types, so the third law test fails.
Give the genuine pair: the Earth pulls the book down while the book pulls the Earth up — both are weight, equal and opposite, on two different objects.
Conclude: Student B is correct — the labelled arrows show balanced forces on a single object, which is Newton's first law territory.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Student B is correct: the two labelled forces act on one object and are of different types, so the diagram illustrates Newton's first law rather than the third.
